passages.text: The MESI cache-coherence protocol assigns each cache line one of four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, or Invalid. When a processor writes to a shared line, it broadcasts an invalidation message so other caches discard their copies before the write proceeds.
passages.evidence: broadcasts an invalidation message

passages.text: A Modified MESI cache line contains newer data than main memory and is therefore dirty. The owning cache must write the modified line back to main memory before eviction. An Exclusive line is clean and has no other cached copies.
passages.evidence: write the modified line back to main memory before eviction

passages.text: The MESI cache protocol records a state for each cache line. When a processor writes to a shared line, it broadcasts an invalidation message so other caches discard their copies before the write proceeds. The writing cache then holds the exclusive valid copy.
passages.evidence: The writing cache then holds the exclusive valid copy

passages.text: The MESI cache protocol records a state for each cache line. When a processor writes to a shared line, it broadcasts an invalidation message so other caches discard their copies before the write proceeds. The line is marked Modified after the write and must be written back later.
passages.evidence: The line is marked Modified after the write

passages.evidence: broadcasts an invalidation message

passages.text: In Raft, a follower starts an election after its randomized election timeout expires without receiving a leader heartbeat. It becomes a candidate, requests votes, and needs votes from a majority of the cluster to become leader.
passages.evidence: needs votes from a majority of the cluster

passages.text: The Raft leader sends log entries to followers in AppendEntries RPCs. The leader commits an entry after a majority of servers have replicated it, then advances its commit index and applies the entry to its state machine.
passages.evidence: commits an entry after a majority of servers have replicated it

passages.text: Huffman coding repeatedly combines the two lowest-frequency nodes in a binary tree. The resulting variable-length code is prefix-free and minimizes the weighted average code length for the supplied symbol frequencies.
passages.evidence: combines the two lowest-frequency nodes

passages.text: Canonical Huffman coding assigns codes from code lengths and symbol order rather than storing each tree edge. A decoder can reconstruct the same prefix-free code table from the ordered symbol lengths.
passages.evidence: assigns codes from code lengths and symbol order

passages.text: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm requires all edge weights to be nonnegative. With a negative edge, a vertex settled as the current minimum can later receive a shorter path, so the greedy finalization step is no longer correct.
passages.evidence: requires all edge weights to be nonnegative

passages.text: For each edge from the selected vertex to a neighbor, Dijkstra's algorithm relaxes the edge by comparing the current distance with the selected distance plus the edge weight. A priority queue selects the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance.
passages.evidence: relaxes the edge by comparing the current distance

passages.text: TCP starts a retransmission timer when it sends data that has not yet been acknowledged. If the retransmission timeout expires, TCP retransmits the unacknowledged segment and updates its estimate of the round-trip time.
passages.evidence: retransmission timeout expires

passages.text: During TCP slow start, the congestion window grows as acknowledgments arrive, approximately doubling each round-trip time until the threshold or a loss event changes the congestion-control phase.
passages.evidence: congestion window grows as acknowledgments arrive

passages.text: A Bloom filter represents set membership with a bit array and several hash functions. To insert an item, it sets the bits selected by those hashes. A query that finds any required bit clear proves the item is absent; a query with all bits set may be a false positive.
passages.evidence: a query with all bits set may be a false positive

passages.text: For a Bloom filter with m bits, n inserted items, and k independent hash functions, the approximate false-positive probability is (1 - exp(-k*n/m))^k. Increasing the bit budget per item can reduce false positives, while too many hash functions set bits more quickly.
passages.evidence: the approximate false-positive probability is (1 - exp(-k*n/m))^k

passages.text: A B-tree stores sorted keys in nodes and uses separator keys in internal nodes to choose the child interval that may contain a search key. Each descent narrows the key range, so lookup visits a path from the root toward a matching leaf.
passages.evidence: separator keys in internal nodes to choose the child interval

passages.text: In a B+ tree, records or record pointers are stored at the leaves, and adjacent leaves are linked in key order. After locating the first key in a range, a scan follows those leaf links instead of returning to the root for every next key.
passages.evidence: a scan follows those leaf links

passages.text: In a TLS 1.3 full handshake, the client and server can use ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key shares to derive a shared secret. Fresh ephemeral keys provide forward secrecy against later compromise of the server's long-term certificate key.
passages.evidence: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key shares to derive a shared secret

passages.text: Each TLS 1.3 peer sends a Finished message containing verify_data derived from the handshake traffic secret and transcript hash. The receiver checks it to authenticate the handshake transcript and confirm both sides derived matching keys.
passages.evidence: verify_data derived from the handshake traffic secret and transcript hash

passages.text: Quicksort partitions an array around a pivot so values on one side compare before the pivot and values on the other side compare after it. It then recursively sorts the partitions. Highly unbalanced partitions can produce quadratic worst-case running time.
passages.evidence: Highly unbalanced partitions can produce quadratic worst-case running time

passages.text: Randomized quicksort chooses a pivot at random, making consistently unbalanced partitions unlikely for a fixed input order. Its expected running time is O(n log n), although its worst case remains O(n^2).
passages.evidence: Its expected running time is O(n log n)
